tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write

Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file outside the working directory that you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your turn is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Read-only access to the user's Zotero research library. For substantive sport-science questions, build a Zotero-first evidence pack before answering. Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. SecondBrain Queue is the priority lane; promotion eligibility is controlled by promotion_scope.

12	---
13	
14	# Armstrong's Seven-Point Physiology Case: Read Only With the Doping Context the 2008 Book Does Not Give
15	
16	**Historical context absent from the source, stated first because it governs how the
17	rest of this entry should be read:** this book was published in 2008. Lance Armstrong
18	was stripped of all seven Tour de France titles (1999-2005) by the USADA "Reasoned
19	Decision" in 2012, following a finding of systematic doping (EPO, blood transfusions,
20	testosterone, corticosteroids) across the span this case study covers. That finding is not
21	in this book and could not have been reflected in it. This is stated as historical fact, not
22	as this entry-writer's opinion or as Eric's judgment; it is not labeled "Inference" because
23	it is not a reasoned inference from the text but an external, independently documented
24	fact about the case's subject. It means the physiological changes below cannot be read
25	as evidence of natural, doping-free long-term adaptation, and the case should not be
26	cited in that way.
27	
28	**What it is** — Issurin presents cyclist Lance Armstrong as a case study in long-term
29	physiological change, based on Coyle (2005), a published laboratory case-report of
30	serial testing from age 21 to 28 (PDF p. 150, printed p. 139; text quote): "From ages 21
31	to 28 he was examined in a physiology laboratory for body composition, maximal
32	oxygen uptake, maximal blood lactate and mechanical efficiency of pedaling." At age 24
33	he was diagnosed with testicular cancer and underwent surgery and a two-year course
34	of treatment including chemotherapy; from ages 27-32 he won the Tour de France six
35	times (per the book's count at time of writing). Over the seven-year span, body weight
36	rose slightly (+0.8 kg) while lean body weight rose more (+1.1 kg). **Verified against
37	the page image (Figure 4.7, PDF p. 151, printed p. 140):** the chart is two twin-axis
38	panels across nine unevenly spaced age points (21.1, 21.4, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28), a
39	hollow-star marker flagging the "medical treatment including chemotherapy" period
40	around age 24-25. Top panel: Heart Rate (left axis, 196-208 beats/min) and VO2max
41	(right axis, 60-85 ml/kg/min); bottom panel: mechanical efficiency (right axis,
42	20-23.5%) and power output at a VO2 of 5 L/min (left axis, 370-420 W), the latter two
43	rising together and roughly linearly across all nine points. The two top-panel series are
44	not unambiguously distinguishable from the rendered image alone (their in-panel labels
45	sit near line peaks without a clear leader-line to one series), so the values below are
46	taken from the book's stated text, not read independently off the chart: **maximum
47	heart rate decreased by 6 beats/min** over the seven years; **VO2max "reached peak
48	value at age 23, declined after medical treatment and did not reach the highest level
49	until age 28"**; **mechanical efficiency increased by 8.8%**; **power output at 5 L/min
50	VO2 increased by 18%**. The book flags that Armstrong's final VO2max, 71 ml/kg/min,
51	is "inferior to the data of elite cyclists which approaches the level of 80 ml/kg/min
52	(Padilla et al., 2000)," and speculates this partly reflects body-weight reduction before
53	races raising relative VO2max further than the absolute lab value shows. Issurin's stated
54	conclusion: "the individual progress of this great athlete was determined not by
55	enlargement of his physiological potential but by its more efficient utilization,"
56	listing hypothesized (not demonstrated) contributors: "pronounced hypertrophy and
57	improved contractility of slow muscle fibers, alteration in myosin ATPase activity,
58	increased cycling efficiency induced by altitude training and enhanced pedaling
59	technique" (PDF p. 150, printed p. 139). The book explicitly calls the "physiological
60	mechanism of this improved muscular efficiency... still unclear."
61	
62	**Why it works** — **The author gives no confirmed mechanism**; he states this
63	directly ("the physiological mechanism of this improved muscular efficiency is still
64	unclear") and lists candidate physiological explanations as speculative, not
65	established. **Inference (post-2012 context, not the book's):** the interpretation
66	problem is worse than an unresolved mechanism, because the underlying data-generating
67	process (systematic doping across this exact age-21-to-32 span, per USADA 2012) is
68	absent from both the book's account and from Coyle (2005), the primary source Issurin
69	cites. Any of the listed changes (mechanical efficiency, power at a fixed VO2, the
70	partial VO2max recovery after chemotherapy) could in principle be influenced by
71	doping practices not measured or disclosed in the primary source; this entry does not
72	assert that they were, only that the book's "individual creativity, self-confidence and
73	athletic wisdom" framing (PDF p. 151, printed p. 140) is not a complete account of the
74	known history.
75	
76	**When to apply** — Limited. The chemotherapy-recovery data point (VO2max
77	declining after cancer treatment, then partially recovering over several years) is the
78	one piece of this case with plausible standalone value, as an illustration that returning
79	to elite endurance performance after major medical treatment is a multi-year process,
80	not a single-season one. Do not use any other part of this case (the "better utilization,
81	not enlarged potential" conclusion, the specific percentage changes, the athlete as a
82	role model for long-term development) without disclosing the doping context above.
83	
84	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested**, and that ceiling is generous
85	given the context problem. This is an n = 1 case study, drawn from a primary source
86	(Coyle, 2005) that has itself drawn public scientific criticism for the same reason
87	(interpreting serial lab data from an athlete later found to have doped throughout the
88	tested period) independent of anything in this book. Do not cite Armstrong's
89	mechanical-efficiency or power gains as evidence for a "utilization, not enlargement"
90	training principle, and do not use this case in any coach- or athlete-facing material
91	without the 2012 finding attached. The Klementiev case
92	([[case-study--klementiev-multiyear-workload-decline-with-podium-longevity]]) is the
93	cleaner example of this book's "long-term progress through utilization, not raw
94	capacity" theme, without the same documented confound.
95	
96	**Example** — **Inference:** if this case is referenced at all in Applied Performance
97	material (e.g., illustrating return-to-elite-performance timelines after major medical
98	treatment), it should be paired with an explicit note on the athlete's subsequent USADA
99	finding, rather than presented as a clean physiology-of-aging or physiology-of-training
100	example.
101	
102	**Related** — [[case-study--klementiev-multiyear-workload-decline-with-podium-longevity]],
103	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]].
104

14	# Klementiev: Training Volume Fell for 19 Years While Podium Results Kept Coming
15	
16	**What it is** — A single-athlete, 19-year longitudinal case: Ivan Klementiev, USSR
17	then Latvian Olympic canoeist, competed across four Olympic cycles, earning one gold
18	and two silver Olympic medals and seven World Championship golds (PDF p. 148,
19	printed p. 137). His total annual paddling volume was tracked by age (Figure 4.6, PDF
20	p. 149, printed p. 138; **verified against the page image**: the chart's peak at age 21,
21	roughly 4,900 km, matches the text's "maximal training volume was attained at age 21
22	when he trained with the USSR national squad"; volume then oscillates with periodic
23	late-quadrennial upticks but trends down through the following years, with the lowest
24	point at age 37, about 1,500 km). Issurin quantifies the decline by quadrennial-cycle
25	average, relative to the first cycle as 100%: **ages 21-24 = 100%; ages 25-28 = 88.2%;
26	ages 29-32 = 77.4%; ages 33-36 = 61%** (PDF p. 148, printed p. 137; text quote).
27	Transition periods lengthened over the same span, "from one to three months during
28	his career." Despite the steady volume decline, "after age 30 [he] won four gold medals
29	at the World Championships and two Olympic silver medals" (PDF p. 149, printed p.
30	138). Issurin's own conclusion: "workload reduction was effectively compensated for
31	by a higher quality of training," which he associates with the athlete's own account
32	(Klementiev, 1994) of "better preparation exploiting Block Periodization, a more
33	conscious and effective selection of exercises, avoidance of non-compatible workload
34	combinations, constant attention to restoration, and the use of a logical program of
35	competition." One deviation in the record is flagged as non-methodological: at age 24
36	(1984), "because of political, not methodological circumstances," Klementiev raced a
37	substitute regatta of socialist countries rather than the Los Angeles Olympics, cutting
38	that season short by a month (Figure 4.6 caption, PDF p. 149, printed p. 138).
39	
40	**Why it works** — The author's own causal claim ("workload reduction was
41	effectively compensated for by a higher quality of training") is stated, not
42	demonstrated: no comparison group, no measured "training quality" variable, and no
43	separation of the Block Periodization approach from the other listed factors (exercise
44	selection, compatibility management, restoration, competition-program logic) or from
45	simple accumulated technical/tactical experience. **The author gives no mechanism**
46	connecting reduced kilometers specifically to Block Periodization as opposed to any
47	other explanation for late-career success, including selection effects (an athlete who
48	stays competitive to age 36 across four Olympiads is, by construction, one of the rare
49	athletes for whom this pattern worked).
50	
51	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college context** — Useful as a
52	citable, named-athlete illustration that declining training volume is not, by itself,
53	evidence of declining performance capacity in an experienced athlete, and that
54	tracking quality/specificity of training rather than raw volume may be the more
55	relevant monitoring question for a veteran player. Pairs directly with
56	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]]'s Table
57	4.5 claim that "motor potential doesn't increase but can be utilized more effectively."
58	
59	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is an n = 1, uncontrolled,
60	retrospective case with no comparison athlete who trained at a constant or rising
61	volume across the same span; it cannot separate the effect of reduced volume, Block
62	Periodization specifically, accumulated technical mastery, opponent turnover, or
63	survivorship (only athletes who remained competitive despite aging appear in this kind
64	of retrospective record; athletes for whom volume reduction did not work are absent
65	from it by definition). It is also a single elite paddler in an individual, cyclic-endurance
66	Olympic sport with a fixed quadrennial target; nothing here generalizes to a college
67	football roster's age range (18-23), position-specific demands, or annual (not
68	quadrennial) competitive cycle. Do not cite this case as evidence that reducing training
69	volume improves or preserves performance in general.
70	
71	**Example** — **Inference:** when a program has a small number of veteran players
72	whose measured training volumes are trending down year over year, Klementiev's case
73	is a reason to check training quality, technical execution, and competition-readiness
74	markers before treating the volume decline itself as a red flag, rather than a license to
75	assume volume reduction is automatically beneficial.
76	
77	**Related** — [[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]],
78	[[case-study--armstrong-physiological-utilization-over-a-doping-era-career]].

14	# Building the Annual Plan: A Nine-Step Sequence, Anchored on Target Competitions
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin gives a fixed nine-step sequence for constructing an annual
17	program (Table 4.2, PDF p. 138, printed p. 127), illustrated stepwise in Figures 4.1-4.4
18	(PDF pp. 139-141, printed pp. 128-130; verified against the page images): (1) determine
19	the target and mandatory competitions, normally taken from the international/national/
20	regional calendar; (2) determine the terms and duration of training stages and periods
21	("in terms of target competitions and methodology"); (3) divide training stages into
22	several meso- and microcycles; (4) plan additional competitions and trials to "finalize
23	the training stages and to diversify the preparatory program"; (5) plan training camps
24	(objectives, terms, places), which also covers altitude preparation (Ch. 5); (6) plan
25	medical and sport-specific tests, with the initial medical exam early season; (7)
26	calculate integrative workload characteristics per month (total mileage, number of
27	lifts, throws, etc.); (8) calculate the same for the full annual cycle, compared against
28	previous years to reveal "weak" points; (9) correct the plan following that review ("as
29	a rule, the first version needs correction and this operation is obligatory"). Figures
30	4.1-4.4 show competitions plotted on four levels (Level A = the single targeted event;
31	Levels B-D = mandatory events of descending importance: national championship,

# Building the Annual Plan: A Nine-Step Sequence, Anchored on Target Competitions

**What it is** — Issurin gives a fixed nine-step sequence for constructing an annual

the target and mandatory competitions, normally taken from the international/national/
regional calendar; (2) determine the terms and duration of training stages and periods
("in terms of target competitions and methodology"); (3) divide training stages into
several meso- and microcycles; (4) plan additional competitions and trials to "finalize
the training stages and to diversify the preparatory program"; (5) plan training camps
(objectives, terms, places), which also covers altitude preparation (Ch. 5); (6) plan
medical and sport-specific tests, with the initial medical exam early season; (7)
calculate integrative workload characteristics per month (total mileage, number of
lifts, throws, etc.); (8) calculate the same for the full annual cycle, compared against
previous years to reveal "weak" points; (9) correct the plan following that review ("as
a rule, the first version needs correction and this operation is obligatory"). Figures
4.1-4.4 show competitions plotted on four levels (Level A = the single targeted event;
Levels B-D = mandatory events of descending importance: national championship,
national cup, regional trials, winter cup), against a month-by-month grid that only
fills in stages/periods, meso/microcycles and training camps in the later figures as each
step is completed. The **optimal design places important competitions at the end of a
training stage** (Fig. 4.2 caption, PDF p. 139, printed p. 128). The plan is not
considered final at step 9: "it must first be reviewed by the administration, colleagues

accumulation and transmutation mesocycles, mostly specialized exercises, strictly
programmed workouts, and the "most effective individually selected restorative
means." The general rule: "training stages within the annual cycle should be similar
but not identical," with mid- and especially late-season stages "more rigorous, more
strictly programmed and better managed" (PDF p. 142, printed p. 131).

Issurin also assigns competition an explicit developmental role even early in the
season, for three stated reasons (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132): it completes each
training stage as "a compulsory component of the training program"; it "breaks the
usual routine and brings out the very important element of athlete spirit"; and it

regular workloads." The competitive program itself should be diversified early season,

season.

best-managed workloads for the pre-competition stages is two-part (PDF p. 142,
printed p. 131): physiologically, it "gives the benefit of higher training responses
prior to the most important events"; psychologically, "it heightens the athletes'
self-confidence as they know that they have additional reserves during the most
stressful phase of their preparation." No further mechanism is given for why the
nine-step sequence itself (as opposed to some other ordering) produces a better plan
than ad hoc planning; the author states only that "coaches put together annual
programs based on their own experience, knowledge and common sense" and that

sequence against an alternative (PDF p. 138, printed p. 127).

technology and reporting section, line 159).

14	# The Quadrennial Cycle: Four Generic Year-Directions, Individualized by Stage Objectives
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin frames multi-year planning around the four-year Olympic
17	cycle, triggered by post-Games analysis: "the challenge of post-Olympic analysis is to
18	internalize positive experiences and reveal the reasons for sub-par performances. Based
19	on the findings, a new preparatory plan is worked out" (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132).
20	He gives a worked example: the Russian national gymnastics team's quadrennial cycle,
21	subdivided into **eight half-year stages**, each with its own general objective (PDF p.
22	144, printed p. 133, cited to Arkajev & Suchilin, 2004): (1) enhancement of
23	sport-specific motor fitness; (2) acquisition of new, highly complex technical skills and
24	their hybrids; (3) updating of competition combinations; (4) further increases in
25	sport-specific motor fitness; (5) enhancement of technical mastery and attaining stable
26	performances; (6) increase in performance quality, stability and stress tolerance; (7)
27	final compilation of competition combinations, endurance for an entire program, and
28	selection of a duplicate Olympic squad; (8) modeling expected competitive conditions,
29	attaining high competitive reliability, and final selection of the Olympic team. Issurin
30	is explicit that this eight-stage division is sport-specific ("a matter of professional
31	competence" depending on conditions), and that "the division of the quadrennial cycle
32	into four annual cycles is the most popular" in general (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133).
33	
34	For the four-annual-cycle version, Table 4.4 (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133; verified
35	against the page image) gives generic year-by-year directions, irrespective of sport:
36	**Year 1** — engagement and examination of new candidates, selection of coaches and
37	staff, updating/correcting training means and methods, remodeling the training
38	repertory, forming team spirit and camaraderie; **Year 2**: further candidate selection
39	and approval, acquisition of new techno-tactical skills, increased training workloads,
40	improved training quality; **Year 3**: attaining maximal training-workload level,
41	approving the Olympic-season annual cycle, determining individual performance
42	characteristics per team member; **Year 4**: stabilizing team make-up (usually with a
43	double Olympic squad), stabilizing workloads at the prior year's level, and approving
44	and stabilizing competitive behavior and performance. Issurin states the third and
45	fourth years "should be very similar since coaches simulate the annual pre-Olympic
46	training design one year before" the Games, though the pre-Olympic (fourth) year's
47	workload is "usually higher than the year before for various reasons," including
48	"greater motivation, better conditions for training and restoration, greater budgets"
49	(PDF p. 146, printed p. 135).
50	
51	**Why it works** — The author gives no controlled-comparison mechanism for why
52	this generic four-year sequence outperforms an alternative structure; it is presented as
53	observed common practice ("the division of the quadrennial cycle into four annual
54	cycles is the most popular") rationalized post hoc by the logic of squad-building
55	(candidate selection and cohesion before workload escalation, workload escalation
56	before stabilization). **Inference:** the underlying logic parallels this library's existing
57	long-term athletic development material: building foundational capacity (team
58	identity, basic skill acquisition) before layering higher, more specific workloads, but
59	Issurin does not state that connection explicitly in this passage.
60	
61	**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college context** — College football has no
62	literal Olympic quadrennium, but the four-year (or five-year, with a redshirt) eligibility
63	window is a structurally similar bounded multi-year cycle with its own roster-cohort
64	logic: Year 1 (true freshman/transfer intake) mapping to Table 4.4's Year 1 emphasis on
65	candidate evaluation and cultural integration; Years 2-3 to skill/technical acquisition
66	and rising training-workload tolerance; a "walk year" (senior or draft-eligible year)
67	to Table 4.4's Year 4 emphasis on stabilized, individualized performance. The
68	gymnastics eight-stage example is a useful illustration that objective-setting per stage
69	should be concrete and sport-specific rather than generic, which is directly usable
70	guidance for building a position-group or class-cohort development plan.
71	
72	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** both the eight-stage
73	gymnastics example and the four-year Table 4.4 are drawn from Olympic individual/
74	team-technical sports with a single fixed quadrennial target and squad continuity
75	controlled by national-team selection, not from a college roster with annual signing
76	classes, transfer portal turnover, and no shared four-year entry cohort (a program's
77	"Year 1" and "Year 4" athletes are present simultaneously every season, unlike a
78	national team's cycle-wide cohort). The table's per-year directions are the author's own
79	applied synthesis of common practice, not a study with an outcome measure; no
80	evidence is given that following this sequence produces better long-term results than
81	an alternative one. The Table 4.4 vs Fig. 4.5 age-cohort content (older/experienced vs.
82	younger-athlete workload differentiation within this same quadrennial frame) is
83	treated separately in
84	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]].
85	
86	**Example** — **Inference:** a position group's four-year development plan borrowing
87	Table 4.4's shape: Year 1 focused on evaluating and culturally onboarding new signees
88	and transfers; Year 2 on techno-tactical (scheme/position) skill acquisition and raising
89	training-load tolerance; Year 3 on maximizing training workload and identifying each
90	player's individual performance profile; Year 4 on stabilizing role, workload, and
91	game-performance consistency for players entering their final season or a likely draft
92	evaluation.
93

95	[[heuristic--older-vs-younger-athlete-quadrennial-workload-differentiation]],
96	[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]].

into four annual cycles is the most popular" in general (PDF p. 144, printed p. 133).

**Year 1** — engagement and examination of new candidates, selection of coaches and
staff, updating/correcting training means and methods, remodeling the training
repertory, forming team spirit and camaraderie; **Year 2**: further candidate selection
and approval, acquisition of new techno-tactical skills, increased training workloads,

14	# Four Stages of Long-Term Preparation, Dosed by Hours and Broken Out by Domain
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin gives the same four-stage long-term development model
17	already in this library from Bompa
18	([[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]]), but adds two things
19	Bompa's entry does not have: an explicit dosing table and a domain-by-domain
20	(technical/physical/tactical/mental) content breakdown per stage. He opens by
21	scoping the topic down: "the athletic career... is highly dependent on the earlier period
22	of long-term preparation that usually begins in childhood. The purview of this chapter
23	restricts consideration of this matter, which is worthy of its own book" (PDF p. 152,
24	printed p. 141). Table 4.6 (PDF p. 152, printed p. 141; **verified against the page
25	image**: the raw text extraction of this table initially dropped a cell, recovered by
26	re-reading the rendered page) gives, per stage: **Preliminary preparation**: 1-3
27	years, 3-4 workouts/week, 45-60 min/workout, 120-170 hours/year; **Initial
28	specialization**: 2-3 years, 4-5 workouts/week, 75-90 min/workout, 250-300
29	hours/year; **Advanced specialization**: 2-3 years, 6-9 workouts/week, 60-120
30	min/workout, 500-750 hours/year; **Sports perfection**: duration "individually
31	dependent," 6-12 workouts/week, 70-150 min/workout, 750-1400 hours/year (cited to
32	Issurin, 1994). Favorable starting ages vary widely by sport (Figure 4.8, PDF p. 153,
33	printed p. 142; verified against the page image): gymnastics and figure skating
34	start roughly ages 7-9; swimming roughly 9-11; team/dual sports ("ball games"),
35	sprint track and field, weightlifting and fencing roughly 11-14; kayaking roughly
36	12-15; rowing roughly 13-16; marathon roughly 13-17; triathlon roughly 13-18
37	(adapted from Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, updated by expert interview). Issurin
38	notes the general trend toward earlier specialization across sport is driven by better
39	child-scaled equipment, training conditions, media popularization, and visible early
40	starters, and that these ranges reflect "worldwide practice" not individual exceptions
41	(PDF p. 153-154, printed p. 142-143).
42	
43	Each stage's content is broken out by four domains in Tables 4.7-4.10 (PDF pp.
44	154-157, printed pp. 143-146): **Preliminary preparation** (Table 4.7): technical:
45	sport-specific and general skill/coordination acquisition; physical: multilateral,
46	all-round development with sport-specific emphasis, raising general training capacity;
47	tactical: acquaintance with basic tactical demands; mental: consolidating interest,
48	forming motivation, "adoption of fundamental moral principles of 'fair play', team
49	spirit." **Initial specialization** (Table 4.8): technical: further sport-specific
50	development, selecting the most favorable discipline/event; physical: more specialized
51	motor-ability development, adapting to sport-typical workloads; tactical: deeper rules
52	and tactics knowledge; mental: self-confidence, will power, "consciousness and
53	responsibility." **Advanced specialization** (Table 4.9): technical: attaining effective,
54	individualized technique, eliminating technical drawbacks; physical: further
55	sport-specific motor-ability gains supporting individualized technique; tactical:
56	individualized tactical/techno-tactical formation; mental: motivation toward
57	excellence, emotional control, mental-regulation skill acquisition. Issurin adds a
58	caution here specific to this stage: "despite increased technical and motor abilities,
59	juniors at this stage are still not completely mature and the use of maximal workloads
60	should be restricted. In particular, administration of highly intense anaerobic glycolitic

# Four Stages of Long-Term Preparation, Dosed by Hours and Broken Out by Domain

**What it is** — Issurin gives the same four-stage long-term development model
already in this library from Bompa
([[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]]), but adds two things
Bompa's entry does not have: an explicit dosing table and a domain-by-domain
(technical/physical/tactical/mental) content breakdown per stage. He opens by
scoping the topic down: "the athletic career... is highly dependent on the earlier period
of long-term preparation that usually begins in childhood. The purview of this chapter
restricts consideration of this matter, which is worthy of its own book" (PDF p. 152,
printed p. 141). Table 4.6 (PDF p. 152, printed p. 141; **verified against the page
image**: the raw text extraction of this table initially dropped a cell, recovered by
re-reading the rendered page) gives, per stage: **Preliminary preparation**: 1-3
years, 3-4 workouts/week, 45-60 min/workout, 120-170 hours/year; **Initial
specialization**: 2-3 years, 4-5 workouts/week, 75-90 min/workout, 250-300
hours/year; **Advanced specialization**: 2-3 years, 6-9 workouts/week, 60-120
min/workout, 500-750 hours/year; **Sports perfection**: duration "individually
dependent," 6-12 workouts/week, 70-150 min/workout, 750-1400 hours/year (cited to
Issurin, 1994). Favorable starting ages vary widely by sport (Figure 4.8, PDF p. 153,
printed p. 142; verified against the page image): gymnastics and figure skating
start roughly ages 7-9; swimming roughly 9-11; team/dual sports ("ball games"),
sprint track and field, weightlifting and fencing roughly 11-14; kayaking roughly
12-15; rowing roughly 13-16; marathon roughly 13-17; triathlon roughly 13-18
(adapted from Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, updated by expert interview). Issurin
notes the general trend toward earlier specialization across sport is driven by better
child-scaled equipment, training conditions, media popularization, and visible early
starters, and that these ranges reflect "worldwide practice" not individual exceptions
(PDF p. 153-154, printed p. 142-143).

Each stage's content is broken out by four domains in Tables 4.7-4.10 (PDF pp.
154-157, printed pp. 143-146): **Preliminary preparation** (Table 4.7): technical:
sport-specific and general skill/coordination acquisition; physical: multilateral,
all-round development with sport-specific emphasis, raising general training capacity;
tactical: acquaintance with basic tactical demands; mental: consolidating interest,
forming motivation, "adoption of fundamental moral principles of 'fair play', team
spirit." **Initial specialization** (Table 4.8): technical: further sport-specific
development, selecting the most favorable discipline/event; physical: more specialized
motor-ability development, adapting to sport-typical workloads; tactical: deeper rules
and tactics knowledge; mental: self-confidence, will power, "consciousness and
responsibility." **Advanced specialization** (Table 4.9): technical: attaining effective,
individualized technique, eliminating technical drawbacks; physical: further
sport-specific motor-ability gains supporting individualized technique; tactical:
individualized tactical/techno-tactical formation; mental: motivation toward
excellence, emotional control, mental-regulation skill acquisition. Issurin adds a
caution here specific to this stage: "despite increased technical and motor abilities,
juniors at this stage are still not completely mature and the use of maximal workloads
should be restricted. In particular, administration of highly intense anaerobic glycolitic
exercises requires complete control because highly qualified juniors can be overly
ambitious in their training routines but not experienced enough in self-regulation of
metabolic and muscular reactions" (PDF p. 155-156, printed p. 144-145). **Sports
perfection** (Table 4.10): technical: further enhancement with individual style;
physical: highest sport-specific ability level and its "improved utilization"; tactical:
tactical creativity, automatized favorite skills; mental: total commitment, highest
self-confidence, mood self-regulation, mental toughness. This fourth stage is "the most
variable in duration": "almost twenty years" for career-long stars like Klementiev and
Armstrong, "four-seven years" for most high-performance athletes (PDF p. 156, printed
p. 145).

**A cross-source contradiction worth recording, not silently resolving:** this
library's Verkhoshansky/Supertraining entry
([[supertraining--verkhoshansky/claim--russian-sport-school-age-guidelines-table]])
gives Soviet sport-school starting ages for some of the same sports that are
considerably earlier than Issurin's Figure 4.8 bands: women's gymnastics 4-5 vs.
Issurin's gymnastics 7-9; swimming 3-7 vs. Issurin's 9-11; weightlifting 10-11 vs.
Issurin's 11-14. Both tables are cited to different Soviet-era sources (Table 1.2 in
Supertraining is unsourced beyond "the Soviet sports-school system"; Figure 4.8 here
is adapted from Platonov & Sakhnovsky, 1988, plus later expert interviews) and neither
book reconciles the gap. Record both; do not average them into a single number.

**Why it works** — Issurin gives no outcome data for the dosing table (Table 4.6)
itself: no citation, no study comparing athletes trained at these hour/frequency bands
against alternative bands. **Inference:** the domain-by-domain content sequencing
(general before specific, tactical/mental development paced alongside physical)
matches this library's existing multilateral-before-specialization rationale
([[periodization--bompa/principle--multilateral-before-specialization]]), but that
connection is this entry's own synthesis, not stated by Issurin in this passage.

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a Baylor context** — The domain-by-domain
tables (4.7-4.10) are a usable template for structuring what "developmental content"
means at each career stage of a college program even though college football players
enter well past Issurin's "preliminary preparation" age band: an incoming freshman's
program content (movement-skill consolidation, general work capacity, tactical
acquaintance with the defense/offense) resembles the "initial specialization" /
"advanced specialization" domain mix more than "sports perfection," which better fits
an established starter. The advanced-specialization caution against maximal
anaerobic-glycolytic loading in not-yet-mature, "overly ambitious" young athletes is a
directly relevant caution for redshirt-freshman and true-freshman conditioning design.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** Table 4.6's specific
hour/frequency bands and Figure 4.8's starting ages are drawn from Olympic individual
and technical sports (gymnastics, swimming, rowing, weightlifting, etc.); American
football is not listed in either this table or the Verkhoshansky comparison table, and no
data source here addresses a contact team sport with a 100+ player roster and
heterogeneous training ages within a single class. The stage-duration bands are the
author's own applied synthesis (cited only to "Issurin, 1994," his own earlier work, not
an independent study), and the domain content lists, while plausible, carry no cited
outcome evidence distinguishing them from an alternative sequencing.

**Example** — **Inference:** using Tables 4.7-4.8's domain content as a checklist for a
true-freshman's first developmental year: technical (movement-pattern competency
before position-specific technique refinement), physical (multilateral work capacity
before narrow specialization), tactical (scheme literacy before disguised assignments),
mental (culture and buy-in before performance-outcome pressure), while applying
Table 4.9's caution against maximal-intensity anaerobic-glycolytic work for players who
are still not fully mature and may be "overly ambitious" relative to their
self-regulation capacity.

[[periodization--bompa/principle--multilateral-before-specialization]],

14	# Sensitive Periods: Ages Where a Motor Ability Trains Fastest, By Sex
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin defines "sensitive periods" as ages when an individual is "more
17	trainable for certain motor abilities than in other times," resting on two stated
18	physiological facts (PDF p. 158, printed p. 147): (a) natural development of motor
19	abilities in children/youth is non-uniform, so sensitive periods yield "the most
20	favorable rate of improvement in certain abilities"; (b) acceleration/deceleration
21	periods for different abilities "do not coincide chronologically." He is explicit that
22	**chronological determination of sensitive periods "remains open to dispute"**: "each
23	fitness component can be characterized by various indices, which can give different
24	(and at times contradictory) chronological trends. This explains the variance in data
25	from different sources" (PDF p. 158, printed p. 147). Figure 4.9 (PDF p. 159, printed p.
26	148; **verified against the page image**, based on Meinel & Schnabel 1976, Martin
27	1980, Volkov 1986) plots the favorable-improvement window per ability, separately for
28	girls and boys, ages 8-18: general coordination roughly 9-12 for both sexes; flexibility
29	roughly 7-10 for both; speed (reaction time) roughly 9-11 for both; speed (movement
30	frequency) roughly 11-13 for both; explosive strength (high/long jump) roughly 11-13
31	in girls but extending to roughly 13-17 in boys; maximal strength roughly 13-17 in
32	girls, roughly 14-18 in boys; strength endurance roughly 11-14 in girls but extending to
33	roughly 11-17 in boys; aerobic endurance roughly 14-17 in girls, roughly 15-18 in
34	boys. The book's running text gives point estimates matching the chart: general
35	motor coordination peaks ages 9-12; flexibility ages 7-10; maximal-speed
36	improvement ages 11-13 in both sexes; reaction time ages 9-11; explosive-strength
37	(jump) improvement peaks 11-13 in girls, 13-17 in boys; aerobic-development
38	practice benefit ages 9-12, with the most favorable sensitive window from age 14 in
39	girls and 15 in boys.
40	
41	The chapter gives partial, explicitly qualified mechanisms for the strength-related
42	periods specifically (PDF pp. 159-160, printed pp. 148-149): jump performance
43	depends on "powerful muscular contractions and body mass," and body mass "increases
44	most noticeably in mid-puberty girls aged 13-15" while their maximal improvement
45	rate occurs earlier, at 11-13; strength gains in mid/late puberty are "directly affected
46	by hormonal changes (maturation) and an increase in muscle mass (growth)"; but
47	"training-induced hypertrophy is much more pronounced in adults in comparison to
48	mid-pubertal or late-pubertal children. Therefore, improvement in neural regulation is
49	the main source of increased explosive and maximal strength" in youth. Androgenic
50	hormones (e.g. testosterone), which "affect anaerobic power production and muscle
51	hypertrophy," are "low in children and only start to increase at ages 12-13 in girls, and
52	13-14 in boys." Aerobic-endurance sensitivity is attributed to "increased body size, and
53	in particular, muscle mass, increased heart volume, total blood volume, and a higher
54	hemoglobin concentration." The chapter closes this section with an explicit safety
55	caution: "the higher sensitivity of children and youth can lead to overload and even
56	injury. This is particularly relevant in training for maximum strength and in power
57	exercises" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149).
58	
59	**Why it works** — The neural-regulation-over-hypertrophy explanation for youth
60	strength gains, and the testosterone-onset ages for anaerobic power/hypertrophy, are
61	standard, independently established developmental physiology, consistent with this
62	library's existing maturation material; that specific mechanism claim can be treated at
63	the `proven` ceiling **for the underlying physiology itself** (androgen-driven
64	hypertrophic capacity rising at puberty; neural adaptation predominating over
65	hypertrophic adaptation before it). The overall age windows in Figure 4.9, however, stay
66	at `supported`: the author himself states the chronological boundaries are disputed
67	across sources, and the figure is a synthesis of three secondary citations (Meinel &
68	Schnabel 1976; Martin 1980; Volkov 1986), none independently checked in this ingest.
69	
70	**When to apply — Inference** — Directly relevant to Applied Performance's role in
71	any camp or clinic work with pre-collegiate athletes, and as background for
72	understanding why a college freshman's training-age deficits in particular abilities
73	(e.g., poor general coordination, limited flexibility) may reflect a missed
74	developmental window rather than a simply "untrained" quality that responds at the
75	same rate an early-developed quality would. The sex-specific timing differences
76	(explosive strength and strength endurance windows running longer in boys; aerobic
77	endurance starting a year later in boys than girls) are a concrete reference for
78	age-and-sex-differentiated youth programming, where Applied Performance interacts
79	with prospective-athlete or camp populations.
80	
81	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** every current Baylor
82	football player is already past every window shown in Figure 4.9 (which stops at age
83	18); this framework describes developmental timing, not a claim about how to train
84	already-matured collegiate athletes, and should not be used to argue that any current
85	ability gap is now unfixable. The author's own caveat applies directly: chronological
86	sensitive-period boundaries are disputed, vary by which index is measured, and come
87	from three secondary sources not independently verified here. Treat the specific age
88	ranges as a useful planning heuristic for youth-facing work, not a precise biological
89	clock.
90	
91	**Example** — **Inference:** a youth combine or camp screening tool that flags,
92	rather than penalizes, a 9-year-old with below-average flexibility or a 14-year-old boy
93	with below-average explosive-strength improvement rate as "inside a sensitive
94	window where targeted work is likely to pay off fastest," consistent with the chapter's
95	framing that these are periods of highest trainability, not fixed ceilings.
96	
97	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
98	[[periodization--bompa/framework--ltad-sequential-model]],
99	[[framework--long-term-preparation-four-stage-model-and-directions]].

13	
14	# Four Talent Factors, Graded by How Fixed They Are
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin defines giftedness as "a predisposition to and a higher
17	trainability for a given activity," treated as "genetically transmitted properties of an
18	individual," such that "a gifted child is potentially a talented athlete" (PDF p. 160,
19	printed p. 149). Citing Williams & Franks (1998) and Williams & Reilly (2000), he
20	organizes talent prediction into four factors, each graded by genetic determination
21	(Table 4.11, PDF p. 161, printed p. 150; **verified against the page image**):
22	**Body build and body composition**: body height, extremity length, foot size
23	(strong); shoulder width, thigh circumference, muscle mass (medium); total body fat
24	(low). **Physiological**: alactic anaerobic power, peak blood lactate, space
25	orientation (high); glycolytic anaerobic power, strength endurance/acidity resistance,
26	flexibility (medium). **Psychological**: self-confidence, anxiety control, motivation,
27	concentration (medium-low), citing Plomin et al. (1994) and Saudino (1997) for a
28	partial heritable component. **Sociological**: parental support, socio-economic
29	background, cultural background, coach-child interaction (heredity independent,
30	though the text adds: "this doesn't mean, however, that they can be changed easily if
31	necessary"). Issurin's practical point in presenting the table this way: "some
32	anthropometrical and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as
33	such, can not be compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict
34	progress in a given sport" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149): the high-heritability rows
35	function as hard constraints on which sports/positions an athlete can realistically excel
36	in, while the low-heritability rows are the ones training and environment can move.
37	
38	The unchangeable-predictor approach is operationalized through "model
39	characteristics" (Bulgakova, 1986): favorable anthropometric/physiological
40	combinations by age category, built from longitudinal study of a large athlete group
41	where a sub-group reaches elite level (citing Vorontsov et al. 1999 and Falk et al.
42	2003 as examples of this being done despite its difficulty), or more commonly from
43	cross-sectional studies comparing less- and more-successful youngsters. Issurin flags
44	the model characteristics' central limitation directly: "the main limitation of this
45	evaluation is in the differing levels of maturity of children that are examined to
46	determine giftedness. Children with slower rates of maturation may be found inferior
47	to more mature teammates but may have greater potential for further progress" (PDF
48	p. 160, printed p. 149). Genetic contribution to training response itself is not constant
49	across a career: citing a young-adult twin study (Bouchard et al., 2000), "the
50	contribution of heredity related factors to training response in an endurance program
51	is different for earlier and later stages of preparation. The initial preparation is less
52	dependent on heredity. However, as athletes progress and approach higher workloads,
53	the genetic control of their training response becomes much stronger" (PDF p. 167,
54	printed p. 156), meaning genetically gifted endurance athletes can be genuinely hard
55	to identify at the earliest stage, not just hard to identify due to maturation confounds.
56	
57	**Why it works** — The heredity-grading in Table 4.11 is presented without a
58	citation for most individual cells (the table itself has no source line beyond the
59	chapter's general references to Williams & Franks/Reilly); it functions as the author's
60	synthesized taxonomy rather than a reported finding with its own effect sizes. The twin
61	study citation (Bouchard et al., 2000) is the one mechanism-level claim in this section
62	with a named, checkable primary source, though it was not independently verified in
63	this ingest.

# Four Talent Factors, Graded by How Fixed They Are

**What it is** — Issurin defines giftedness as "a predisposition to and a higher
trainability for a given activity," treated as "genetically transmitted properties of an
individual," such that "a gifted child is potentially a talented athlete" (PDF p. 160,
printed p. 149). Citing Williams & Franks (1998) and Williams & Reilly (2000), he
organizes talent prediction into four factors, each graded by genetic determination
(Table 4.11, PDF p. 161, printed p. 150; **verified against the page image**):
**Body build and body composition**: body height, extremity length, foot size
(strong); shoulder width, thigh circumference, muscle mass (medium); total body fat
(low). **Physiological**: alactic anaerobic power, peak blood lactate, space
orientation (high); glycolytic anaerobic power, strength endurance/acidity resistance,
flexibility (medium). **Psychological**: self-confidence, anxiety control, motivation,
concentration (medium-low), citing Plomin et al. (1994) and Saudino (1997) for a
partial heritable component. **Sociological**: parental support, socio-economic
background, cultural background, coach-child interaction (heredity independent,
though the text adds: "this doesn't mean, however, that they can be changed easily if
necessary"). Issurin's practical point in presenting the table this way: "some
anthropometrical and physiological variables are highly dependent on heredity and as
such, can not be compensated for by other personal traits. Thus, they can restrict
progress in a given sport" (PDF p. 160, printed p. 149): the high-heritability rows
function as hard constraints on which sports/positions an athlete can realistically excel
in, while the low-heritability rows are the ones training and environment can move.

The unchangeable-predictor approach is operationalized through "model
characteristics" (Bulgakova, 1986): favorable anthropometric/physiological
combinations by age category, built from longitudinal study of a large athlete group
where a sub-group reaches elite level (citing Vorontsov et al. 1999 and Falk et al.
2003 as examples of this being done despite its difficulty), or more commonly from
cross-sectional studies comparing less- and more-successful youngsters. Issurin flags
the model characteristics' central limitation directly: "the main limitation of this
evaluation is in the differing levels of maturity of children that are examined to
determine giftedness. Children with slower rates of maturation may be found inferior
to more mature teammates but may have greater potential for further progress" (PDF
p. 160, printed p. 149). Genetic contribution to training response itself is not constant
across a career: citing a young-adult twin study (Bouchard et al., 2000), "the
contribution of heredity related factors to training response in an endurance program
is different for earlier and later stages of preparation. The initial preparation is less
dependent on heredity. However, as athletes progress and approach higher workloads,
the genetic control of their training response becomes much stronger" (PDF p. 167,
printed p. 156), meaning genetically gifted endurance athletes can be genuinely hard
to identify at the earliest stage, not just hard to identify due to maturation confounds.

**Why it works** — The heredity-grading in Table 4.11 is presented without a
citation for most individual cells (the table itself has no source line beyond the
chapter's general references to Williams & Franks/Reilly); it functions as the author's
synthesized taxonomy rather than a reported finding with its own effect sizes. The twin
study citation (Bouchard et al., 2000) is the one mechanism-level claim in this section
with a named, checkable primary source, though it was not independently verified in
this ingest.

**When to apply — Inference** — Directly relevant to how Applied Performance and
recruiting staff frame "traits we can develop" versus "traits we are selecting for":
Table 4.11's strong/medium/low-heritability split is a usable lens for separating
recruiting criteria (anthropometrics, alactic power, space orientation: closer to fixed)
from developmental targets (glycolytic capacity, strength endurance, flexibility,
psychological skills: more trainable), while the maturation-confound caution is a
direct argument for tracking training age and biological maturation alongside any
"talent" read on a young or first-year athlete, consistent with
[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]].

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference, population caveat:** this taxonomy and its
heritability gradings are drawn from Olympic individual-sport talent-ID research
(swimming, track, rowing-type literature per the cited authors); American football's
position-specific demands are not addressed, and no cell in Table 4.11 is football-
specific. The heritability labels ("strong," "medium," "high," "medium-low") are
qualitative and unsourced at the individual-cell level in this passage; treat them as the
author's organizing synthesis, not as quantified heritability estimates. The
maturation-confound caution applies most directly to youth/pre-collegiate evaluation
and is less relevant once an athlete has finished growth, though the same caution about
mistaking current-training-age effects for fixed talent still applies to a true freshman.

**Example** — **Inference:** using the four-factor split as a talking-point framework
when a coach asks whether a trait is coachable: anthropometrics and alactic power
profile are closer to "select for, don't expect to build"; strength endurance,
flexibility, and psychological-skill factors are closer to "build through training and
sport psychology support," while sociological factors (family support, coach-athlete
relationship) sit entirely outside a strength staff's typical intervention but are named
here as real, modifiable contributors to development.

[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]].

14	# 320 US Select Swimmers: Early Maturers Look Best Young, Late Maturers Stay in the Sport
15	
16	**What it is** — Issurin cites a cross-sectional study of 320 swimmers, ages 11-18,
17	participants in the USA Select Program, examined for "biological age, anthropometric
18	status, muscle strength and power, swim-specific abilities and performance time" (PDF
19	p. 162, printed p. 151, citing Troup et al., 1991). The stated finding: "the best athletes
20	at younger ages are usually more mature than their less successful counterparts while
21	the best athletes in the older ages are mostly on-time maturers (80% of the US
22	National team) or late maturers (18% of the team)." The book's own gloss on the
23	authors' interpretation: "the authors suggest that high performing late maturers have
24	better chances of remaining involved with the sport for longer periods" (PDF p. 162,
25	printed p. 151).
26	
27	**A tension worth recording, not resolving silently:** this case sits in some
28	tension with the chapter's own general framing of talent identification around
29	"unchangeable predictors, most often associated with anthropometric and
30	physiological factors" (Table 4.11 and the surrounding text,
31	[[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]]). If the athletes who look
32	best at younger ages (by early anthropometric/physiological maturation) are
33	disproportionately *not* the ones who remain in, or lead, the sport by the older age
34	bracket, then early anthropometric standing is a poor stand-alone predictor of who
35	eventually succeeds, which is consistent with, and directly reinforces, Issurin's own
36	separately stated maturation-confound caution ("children with slower rates of
37	maturation may be found inferior to more mature teammates but may have greater
38	potential for further progress," PDF p. 160, printed p. 149) rather than contradicting it.
39	The tension is between the chapter's early framing (identify talent via largely fixed,
40	heredity-linked traits) and this case's finding (the early-identified "best" are not
41	reliably the eventual best), and the author does not explicitly connect the two passages
42	himself.
43	
44	**Why it works** — **The author gives no mechanism** beyond restating the study
45	authors' own suggested interpretation (late maturers "remaining involved... for longer
46	periods," implying either better long-term retention, a longer competitive runway once
47	peers catch up physically, or both). No causal pathway (psychological, physiological, or
48	selection/dropout-driven) is specified in the passage.
49	
50	**When to apply — Inference** — Directly relevant caution for any recruiting or
51	early talent-evaluation process: a young athlete who is currently outperforming peers
52	due to early physical maturation is not reliably the athlete who will still be
53	outperforming peers once maturation differences equalize, and a currently
54	underperforming, physically less-mature athlete of the same chronological age may
55	have a longer developmental runway. This is a concrete, citable data point supporting
56	[[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]]'s general caution against
57	treating early-maturer dominance as durable talent.
58	
59	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is a single cross-sectional
60	study (not longitudinal: it compares different athletes at younger and older ages, not
61	the same athletes tracked over time) in one sport (swimming), one country's development
62	pipeline (USA Select Program, 1991), with no report of effect size, statistical test, or
63	confidence interval in the passage as retold. It should not be read as showing that any
64	individual late-maturing young athlete will become elite, only that the population-level
65	pattern the study reports runs counter to naively selecting only the most physically
66	advanced young athletes. The finding has not been checked here against the original
67	Troup et al. (1991) publication; only the book's retelling was read.
68	
69	**Example** — **Inference:** when evaluating a cohort of high-school or youth
70	prospects, treating early physical dominance as one input rather than the deciding
71	factor, and tracking (rather than deprioritizing) athletes who are chronologically
72	age-matched but physically less mature, consistent with this case's reported pattern
73	that late maturers were disproportionately represented among the eventual national
74	team.
75	
76	**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]],
77	[[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]],
78	[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]].

# 35 Elite Soviet Paddlers: What Age-14-15 Performance Looked Like Before They Were Elite

**What it is** — Issurin cites a retrospective interview study of 35 "world leading
canoe-kayak paddlers who took part in the USSR National team and earned medals in
the Olympic Games and World Championships within eight years prior to the study"
(PDF p. 163, printed p. 152, citing Sozin, 1986). Respondents were interviewed about
their official performance results from ages 14-15, "the end of their first year of
long-term preparation"; athletes who began preparation later were excluded from the
analysis. **Verified against the page image (Figure 4.10, PDF p. 163, printed p. 152):**
performance time on a 500-m course is plotted by two-year age band (14-15 through
18-19) for three groups (kayak-males, kayak-females, canoeists), all three showing a
steep improvement curve from roughly 140-152 seconds at 14-15 down to roughly
102-120 seconds by 18-19, with kayak-males consistently fastest across every age band
and kayak-females and canoeists tracking close together. The book frames the result as
a usable historical benchmark rather than a fixed standard: "despite the substantial
improvement of paddles and boats in the two decades since this study was conducted,
the results achieved by outstanding athletes in the earlier stages of their preparation
remain relevant to this day for evaluation of giftedness in today's young athletes" (PDF
p. 163, printed p. 152).

**Why it works** — **The author gives no mechanism** connecting age-14-15
performance time to eventual elite status; the case is presented purely as a descriptive
benchmark curve, not as a validated predictive model (no reported correlation,
sensitivity, or false-positive/false-negative rate for using these times to screen
today's youngsters). Issurin's own claim that equipment-era changes do not invalidate
the benchmark is asserted, not tested against any comparison of era-adjusted times.

**When to apply — Inference** — As a template, not as transferable numbers: the
approach of interviewing an already-elite cohort about their own performance at a
fixed early-career age point, to build a retrospective reference curve for evaluating
today's youngsters, is a reusable talent-identification method independent of the
specific canoe-kayak times. It illustrates the general "model characteristics" approach
named earlier in the chapter (Bulgakova, 1986,
[[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]]) with a concrete worked
example of how such a benchmark curve is actually built and reported.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence is untested.** This is a retrospective,
survivorship-selected sample: all 35 respondents were already-successful medalists at
the time of interview, so the study cannot say what fraction of 14-15-year-olds with
similar performance times failed to reach the same level (no comparison group of
similarly-fast 14-15-year-olds who did not become elite). It is also sport- and era-specific
(1970s-80s Soviet canoe-kayak, single national federation, pre-modern boat and
paddle equipment) with no cited data from any other sport or country, and the book's
own claim that "the results... remain relevant to this day" is the author's assertion, not
a re-tested comparison against a current cohort. Do not use the specific second-count
benchmarks as a screening cutoff for any current sport without independent
verification.

**Example** — **Inference:** the method (not the numbers) could be adapted for a
sport Applied Performance evaluates by asking current or recent elite alumni for their
own testing numbers at a fixed early developmental checkpoint (e.g. end of a true
freshman year), building an internal reference curve for how "what elite eventually
looked like at this checkpoint" compares to a current prospect, while explicitly
tracking that such a curve, built only from athletes who succeeded, cannot say how
many similarly-scoring peers did not.

**Related** — [[framework--athletic-talent-four-factor-heredity-model]],
[[heuristic--dual-approach-initial-level-and-improvement-rate-giftedness]],
[[case-study--troup-swimmers-maturation-timing-and-longevity]].

The general tendency is to gradually increase workload specialization and 
mobilization of hidden reserves towards the target competition. The general rule in 
Block Periodization is that the training stages within the annual cycle should be 
similar but not identical. The mid season and particularly late season stages should be 
more rigorous, more strictly programmed and better managed. It is highly desirable 
that the most effective training and restorative means and drill combinations be 
reserved for the crucial periods in annual preparation. Physiologically, this gives the 
benefit of higher training responses prior to the most important events.

# Building the Annual Plan: A Nine-Step Sequence, Anchored on Target Competitions

**What it is** — Issurin gives a fixed nine-step sequence for constructing an annual
program (Table 4.2, PDF p. 138, printed p. 127), illustrated stepwise in Figures 4.1-4.4
(PDF pp. 139-141, printed pp. 128-130; verified against the page images): (1) determine
the target and mandatory competitions, normally taken from the international/national/
regional calendar; (2) determine the terms and duration of training stages and periods
("in terms of target competitions and methodology"); (3) divide training stages into
several meso- and microcycles; (4) plan additional competitions and trials to "finalize
the training stages and to diversify the preparatory program"; (5) plan training camps
(objectives, terms, places), which also covers altitude preparation (Ch. 5); (6) plan
medical and sport-specific tests, with the initial medical exam early season; (7)
calculate integrative workload characteristics per month (total mileage, number of
lifts, throws, etc.); (8) calculate the same for the full annual cycle, compared against
previous years to reveal "weak" points; (9) correct the plan following that review ("as
a rule, the first version needs correction and this operation is obligatory"). Figures
4.1-4.4 show competitions plotted on four levels (Level A = the single targeted event;
Levels B-D = mandatory events of descending importance: national championship,
national cup, regional trials, winter cup), against a month-by-month grid that only
fills in stages/periods, meso/microcycles and training camps in the later figures as each
step is completed. The **optimal design places important competitions at the end of a
training stage** (Fig. 4.2 caption, PDF p. 139, printed p. 128). The plan is not
considered final at step 9: "it must first be reviewed by the administration, colleagues
and athletes and with repeated analysis, will lead to corrections" (PDF p. 141, printed
p. 130) before it "receives the final version status that is used for realization."

Layered on this procedure is a seasonal content trend (Table 4.3, PDF p. 142, printed p.
131; verified against the page image): early season favors continuous/uniform/
alternating methods in the accumulation mesocycle and a wide range of fitness
exercises, more individual workouts, and general restorative means (stretching,
relaxation, low-intensity aerobics); mid-season narrows toward interval methods, a
restricted exercise range, and adds physiotherapy/massage/mental training/nutritional
supplements; late season is "strictly programmed interval exercises" in both
accumulation and transmutation mesocycles, mostly specialized exercises, strictly
programmed workouts, and the "most effective individually selected restorative
means." The general rule: "training stages within the annual cycle should be similar
but not identical," with mid- and especially late-season stages "more rigorous, more
strictly programmed and better managed" (PDF p. 142, printed p. 131).

Issurin also assigns competition an explicit developmental role even early in the
season, for three stated reasons (PDF p. 143, printed p. 132): it completes each
training stage as "a compulsory component of the training program"; it "breaks the
usual routine and brings out the very important element of athlete spirit"; and it
"provides athletes with extraordinary training stimuli that can not be obtained from
regular workloads." The competitive program itself should be diversified early season,
narrowed toward event-specific standards mid-season, and strictly event-specific late
season.

**Why it works** — The author's own stated rationale for reserving the most rigorous,
best-managed workloads for the pre-competition stages is two-part (PDF p. 142,
printed p. 131): physiologically, it "gives the benefit of higher training responses
prior to the most important events"; psychologically, "it heightens the athletes'
self-confidence as they know that they have additional reserves during the most
stressful phase of their preparation." No further mechanism is given for why the
nine-step sequence itself (as opposed to some other ordering) produces a better plan
than ad hoc planning; the author states only that "coaches put together annual
programs based on their own experience, knowledge and common sense" and that
Block Periodization "implies specific demands to planning" without benchmarking the
sequence against an alternative (PDF p. 138, printed p. 127).

**When to apply — Inference, mapped to a college football calendar** — The Level
A/B/C/D competition tiers map reasonably well onto a football master calendar: Level
A as the postseason target (playoff/bowl window), Level B as rivalry or
conference-championship-implication games, Level C/D as the rest of the regular-season
slate. Step 1 (fix the target and mandatory events) and step 5 (plan camps, including
fall camp) are directly usable planning anchors for Applied Performance's annual
calendar-building work with the sport coaching staff. The step-7/8 "integrative
workload characteristics per month, compared with previous years" is a concrete,
citable structure for what a season-over-season GPS/load report should track, distinct
from (and a possible template for) the currently undocumented "standardized
weekly/monthly coach-facing reporting" gap named in `method-baseline.md` (Data,
technology and reporting section, line 159).

**When NOT to apply** — This is Issurin's own applied planning template for an
individual/dual-sport Olympic calendar with a single clearly ranked target competition
determined well in advance; it is not derived from any comparative study of planning
methods (no control condition, no outcome data for the sequence itself). **Inference,
population caveat:** college football's postseason destination (which bowl, or which
playoff round) is not known when the annual plan is first built, which weakens step 1's
premise that the target competition can be fixed at the top of the sequence the way an
Olympic Trials date or a World Championship date can be; the plan has to accommodate
a moving Level-A target rather than a scheduled one. The "optimal design places
important competitions at the end of a training stage" (Fig. 4.2) also assumes the coach
controls stage boundaries around the competition calendar; in football the
competition calendar (one game almost every week, in season) is closer to Issurin's
"competitive microcycle" pattern described elsewhere in this book than to a plan with
discrete preparation stages ending in isolated target events.

**Example** — **Inference:** using the nine-step sequence as a working checklist for a
Baylor football annual calendar: fix the bowl/playoff-window target and the
conference-championship-implication games (step 1); block out fall camp, the
regular-season in-season maintenance stage, and the bowl-prep stage (step 2-3); slot
non-conference "trial" games and any scrimmages (step 4); place fall camp and any
summer training windows (step 5); align the pre-participation physical and preseason
testing battery to early season (step 6); build a month-by-month GPS/load-volume
summary (step 7-8) and review it against the prior season before finalizing (step 9).

[[framework--accumulation-transmutation-realization-mesocycles]],
[[framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]],
[[framework--pre-competitive-microcycle-tuning]].
